The Folia meets Liszt’s Spanish reminiscences
La Folia tradition → Franz Liszt · documented

The Dies irae is a medieval chant for the Day of Judgement whose opening notes became a musical sign of death. Its recognisable outline lets composers summon terror, turn a dance sinister, or pit mortal fear against consolation.

B♭–A–C–B♮ spells Bach in German note names, turning a surname into a four-note musical signature. Later composers used its tightly packed semitones both to salute Bach and to test what their own counterpoint could make of his name.

The Tristan chord is the four-note sonority near the opening of Wagner’s prelude whose continuation keeps a firm arrival out of reach. It became a shorthand for unresolved longing that later composers could embrace, remember or mischievously puncture.

A lament bass falls step by step through a fourth, sometimes filling the descent with chromatic notes. Returning beneath changing voices, it can make grief feel inescapable without requiring every lament to quote the same melody.

La Folia is an inherited dance framework whose familiar minor-key melody and harmonic circuit invite successive variations. Its fixed outline lets composers display wildly different rhythms, textures and virtuosity while listeners keep their bearings.

Beethoven’s Ode to Joy melody carries Schiller’s appeal to human fellowship into the finale of the Ninth Symphony. Its plain, singable shape made it available for virtuoso transcription, symphonic argument and public ceremonies far beyond the concert hall.

Frère Jacques is a round whose repeated phrases make its tune immediately recognisable even when the surrounding music changes. Mahler’s First Symphony turns that familiarity into estrangement by placing a minor-mode version inside a funeral procession.
